text: You already know how to stand up infrastructure with Terraform and run workloads on Kubernetes. The next skill is knowing what's actually happening inside that infrastructure once real traffic hits it. Monitoring watches known signals against known thresholds. Observability is the bigger property: can you answer a question you never thought to ask in advance, using only the telemetry the system already produced? That answer comes from three pillars working together, not any one of them alone.

Metrics are numeric measurements sampled over time, pre-aggregated and cheap to store, which is exactly what makes them the right first signal to alert and dashboard on — they tell you something is wrong, fast. Logs are discrete, timestamped records of single events, keeping the full detail a metric throws away — they tell you what exactly happened. Traces follow one request across every service it touches, as linked spans sharing a trace ID — they tell you where in that chain the time actually went.

Here's a real alerting query: histogram_quantile at the 99th percentile over checkout's request duration histogram, firing when it crosses half a second. That's a metric doing its job — scanning across every service in seconds to show you which one bent out of its normal band. What it can't tell you is why. A graph climbing at 14:02 tells you something broke at 14:02, not which request or which dependency was slow.

A trace reconstructs the whole journey under one trace ID, broken into spans — one per hop, each with its own duration and parent. Here, checkout-service took 402 milliseconds, but drilling into its spans shows inventory-service alone ate 380 of them. Neither a metrics dashboard nor one service's own logs in isolation would have shown you that — only the trace makes the call chain visible end to end.

Walk a real page: an alert fires because a metric crossed its threshold. You don't know why yet, so you pull a trace for a slow sample and see which span dominates — inventory-service. Now you know where, but not why, so you pull that service's logs filtered to the trace ID and find the actual exception. Metrics found it, the trace localized it, logs explained it. Drop any one pillar and the investigation stalls.

That's the three pillars: metrics for is something wrong, logs for what happened, traces for where the time went, and all three needed together on a real incident. Next lesson goes deep on logs specifically — turning a log line from something a human skims into something a machine can actually query.
